Heike Monogatari - Anonymous - 12

建禮 門院 は 、 東山 の 麓 、 吉田 の 邊 なる 所 にぞ 、 立入 せ 給ひ ける 。 中納 言法 印慶 惠 と 申ける 奈良 法師 の 坊 なり けり 。 住荒 し て 年 久しう 成け れ ば 庭 に は 草 深く 、 軒 に は し の ぶ茂 れり 。 簾たえ 閨露 は にて 、 雨 風 たまる べう も なし 。 花 は 色々 匂 へ ども 主 と 憑む 人 も なく 、 月 は 夜 な ／ ＼ さ し 入れ ども 、 詠め て 明す主 も なし 。 昔 は 玉 の 臺 を 磨き 、 錦 の 帳 に 纒れ て 、 明し暮し給ひ し が 、 今 は 有 と し 有 人 に は 、 皆 別 果て て 、 あさま しげ なる 朽坊 に 入ら せ給ひ ける 御心 の 中 お し は から れ て 哀 なり 。 魚 の 陸 に 上れる が 如く 、 鳥 の 巣 を 離たる が 如し 。 さる まゝ に は 、 憂りし波 の 上 、 船 の 中 の 御住 ひ も 、 今 は 戀しうぞ思 召す 。 蒼波 路遠 し 、 思 を 西海千 里 の 雲 に 寄せ 、 白屋 苔 深く し て 、 涙 東山 一庭 の 月 に 落つ 。 悲し とも 云 ばかり なし 。

Translation: The retired Empress Kenreimon entered the place at the foot of Higashiyama, near Yoshida. It was the monastery of the Nara monk known as the Chūnagon Hōin Kekei. Having lived there in desolation for many years, the garden was overgrown with deep grass, and the eaves were thick with creeping vines. The blinds were broken, and the dew of the sleeping chamber was undisturbed; there was no place to shelter from rain or wind. Though flowers of various kinds emitted their scents, there was no one to rely upon as a host; though the moon shone in night after night, there was no host to compose poems and greet the dawn. In former days, she polished the jade platform and was wrapped in brocade curtains, living from morning to evening, but now, to those who are worthy and those who are not, all has come to an end, and her heart, which entered the pitifully dilapidated monastery, is perceived and is sorrowful. It is like a fish washed up on land, like a bird that has left its nest. Under such circumstances, she now longs to dwell in the boat upon the troubled waves. The path of blue waves is far; she sends her thoughts to the clouds of the Western Sea a thousand ri away, while her white house is covered in deep moss, and her tears fall upon the moon in the single courtyard of Higashiyama. There is nothing but sorrow to be spoken.

See notes

かく て 女院 は 文治 元年 五月 一 日 、 御ぐし 下さ せ 給けり 。 御戒 の 師 に は 、 長樂 寺 の 阿證 房 の 上人 印誓 とぞ 聞え し 。 御 布施 に は 、 先帝 の 御 直衣 なり 。 今 は の 時 まで 召さ れ たり けれ ば 、 其 移り 香 も いまだ うせ ず 。 御 形見 に 御 覽 ぜん と て 、 西國 より 遙々 と 都 迄 持せ 給ひ たり けれ ば 、 如何 なら ん 世 まで も 、 御身 を はな たじ と こそ 思召 さ れ けれども 、 御 布施 に なり ぬ べき 物 の なき 上 、 且 は 彼 御 菩提 の 爲 と て 、 泣々 取出 さ れ 給 ひけり 。 上人是 を 給 て 、 何 と 奏 する 旨 も なく し て 、 墨染 の 袖 を 絞り つつ 泣々 罷 出 で られ けり 。 此御 衣 を ば幡 に 縫 て 、 長 樂 寺 の 佛前 に 懸ら れ ける とぞ 聞え し 。

Translation: Thus, on the first day of the fifth month of the first year of Bunji, the retired Empress passed away. It was heard that the master of her precepts was Shōshōbō no Shōin of Chōraku-ji Temple. Her offering was the direct robe of the late emperor. Since she had been summoned until that time, her lingering scent remained. Because she had brought it all the way from the western provinces to the capital, intending to view it as a keepsake, she had thought that even in the coming generations she would not part with her body, but since there was no other object suitable to become an offering, and furthermore, for the sake of his spiritual repose, she tearfully took it out. The monk, receiving this, without making any report, wrung out the sumi-dyed sleeve and tearfully departed. It was heard that this robe was sewn into a banner and hung before the Buddha at Chōraku-ji Temple.

See notes

Thus, on the first day of the fifth month of the first year of Bunji, the retired Empress passed away. It was heard that the master of her precepts was Shōshōbō no Shōin of Chōraku-ji Temple. Her offering was the direct robe of the late emperor. Since she had been summoned until that time, her lingering scent remained. Because she had brought it all the way from the western provinces to the capital, intending to view it as a keepsake, she had thought that even in the coming generations she would not part with her body, but since there was no other object suitable to become an offering, and furthermore, for the sake of his spiritual repose, she tearfully took it out. The monk, receiving this, without making any report, wrung out the sumi-dyed sleeve and tearfully departed. It was heard that this robe was sewn into a banner and hung before the Buddha at Chōraku-ji Temple.

Comment: The phrase '墨染の袖を絞りつつ' (while wringing out the ink-dyed sleeve) depicts the monk's attempt to conceal his weeping by wiping tears with his sleeves, a visual trope in medieval Buddhist hagiography that contrasts the monk's ascetic status (wearing somber ink-dyed robes) with the overwhelming emotional gravity of the ritual act. This specific imagery of 'wringing' (shibori) the sleeve is a distinct rhetorical device marking the climax of the narrative, emphasizing the physical manifestation of grief that transcends the monk's duty to remain composed.

See notes

女院 は 十 五 にて 女御 の 宣旨 を 下さ れ 、 十 六 にて 后妃 の 位 に そな はり 、 君 王 の 側 に 候 は せ 給ひ て 、 朝 に は 朝政 を 勸め 、 夜 は 夜 を 專 に し 給 へり 。 二十 二 にて 皇子 御 誕生 有 て 、 皇太子 に 立ち 、 位 に つか せ給 し かば 、 院號 蒙ら せ 給ひ て 、 建禮 門院 と ぞ申ける 。 入道 相國 の 御 娘 なる 上 、 天子 の 國 母 にて まし まし けれ ば 世 の 重し 奉る 事斜 なら ず 。 今年 は 二十 九 にぞ なら せ 給ふ 。 桃李 の 御粧 猶濃 か に 、 芙蓉 の 御容 未だ 衰 さ せ 給 はね ど も 、 翡翠 の 御かざ し つけ て も 何 に か は せ さ せ 給ふ べき なれ ば 、 遂 に 御 樣 を か へ さ せ 給ひ 、 浮世 を 厭ひ 、 實 の 道 に 入せ 給 へ ども 、 御歎き は 更に 盡せ ず 。 人人 今 は かく とて海 に 沈し 有 樣 、 先帝 、 二 位 殿 の 御 面影 、 如何 なら ん 世 まで も 忘 が たく思食す に 露 の 御命 何 し に 今 まで ながら へ て 、 かゝる 憂 目 を 見る らん と 思食め し 續け て 御 涙 せき あへさ せ 給 はず 。 五月 の 短夜 なれ ど も 明しかね さ せ 給 ひつ ゝ 、 自打 睡 ませ 給 はね ば 、 昔 の 事 は 夢 に だ に も 御 覽ぜ ず 。 壁 に 背ける 殘 の 燈の 影幽 に 、 夜 も す がら 窓 打暗き 雨 の 音ぞ さび しかり ける 。 上陽 人 が 上 陽宮 に 閉られ けん 悲み も 、 是に は 過じ とぞ 見え し 。 昔 を 忍ぶ 妻 と なれ と て や 、 本 の 主 の 移し 栽 たり けん 花 橘 の 軒 近く 風 なつ か しう 香り ける に 、 山郭 公 二 聲 三 聲 音信 け れ ば 、 女院 ふるき 事 なれ 共 、 思召 出 で て 、 御 硯 の 蓋 に かう ぞ遊 ば さ れ ける 。

Translation: The Empress Dowager, at the age of fifteen, was granted the title of Nyogo; at sixteen, she ascended to the rank of Kōhi, and was allowed to attend the Emperor, advising him on morning governance and dedicating herself to night duties. At twenty-two, she gave birth to a Prince, who was established as Crown Prince, and upon being installed as Emperor, she received the title of In and was called the Kenreimon-in. As the daughter of the Retired Prime Minister and the Mother of the Emperor, she was held in great esteem by the world. This year, she turns twenty-nine. Her peach and plum-like beauty remains vivid, and her lotus-like countenance has not yet begun to fade, yet even with the finest jade ornaments, she could not help but feel that her appearance could not be maintained; thus, she finally changed her appearance, grew weary of the floating world, and entered the path of the True Way, yet her sighs were far from exhausted. Seeing how everyone now sinks into the sea of sorrow, she thought with great difficulty how the former Emperor and the Second Rank Lady might be forgotten even in the world to come, and wondered how long her dew-like life would continue to witness such sorrowful scenes, but she could not restrain her tears from falling. Although it was a short summer night, she could not sleep, and since she did not drift into a light doze, she did not even see the past in dreams. The shadow of the remaining lamp leaning against the wall was dim, and the sound of the dark rain beating against the window all night was indeed desolate. Even the sorrow of the Upper Yang Lady confined in the Upper Yang Palace did not surpass this. Thinking of herself as a wife who remembered the past, she pondered whether the flower of the hawthorn, transplanted near the eaves of the original master's house, had grown so dear to the wind that it smelled nostalgically; when the Mountain Crow's two and three calls could no longer be heard, the Empress Dowager, though it was an old matter, brought forth her thoughts and played with the lid of the inkstone in this manner.

See notes

Comment: The phrase '山郭公二聲三聲音信ければ' (yamakugutsu ni koe san koe uketsukeba) relies on a specific classical allusion to the Japanese legend of the 'Mountain Cuckoo' (yamakugutsu or hototogisu), whose cry was believed to be a message from the dead or a harbinger of sorrow. In this context, the repetition of 'ni koe' (two voices) and 'san koe' (three voices) followed by 'uketsukeba' (receiving/accepting the message) suggests the bird's cry is interpreted as a direct summons or a confirmation of the Lady's deep, inescapable melancholy, transforming a natural sound into a narrative catalyst for her recalling the past. This usage elevates the bird from a mere seasonal marker to an active agent in the psychological landscape of the passage.

See notes

女房 達 は 、 さのみ たけく 、 二 位 殿 、 越前 の 三位 の 上 の 樣 に 、 水 の 底 に も 沈み 給 ね ば 、 武士 の 荒け なき に とら は れ て 、 舊里 に 歸り 、 若き も 老たる も樣 を か へ 、 形 を やつ し 、 在 に も あら れ ぬ 有樣 にてぞ 、 思ひ も かけ ぬ谷 の 底 、 岩 の 挾間 に 明し暮し給ひ ける 。 住し 宿 は 皆 烟 と 上り に しかば 、 空しき 跡 のみ 殘り て 、 茂き野邊 と 成つ ゝ 、 見馴し 人 の 問くる も なし 。 仙家 より 歸 て 、 七 世 の 孫 に 逢 けん も 、 かく や と 覺え て 哀也 。

Translation: The ladies, not being as valiant as the Lady of the Second Rank or the Lady of the Third Rank of Echizen, were not able to sink into the depths of the water; they were captured by the rough warriors, returned to their old home, and whether young or old, they changed their appearance, disfigured their forms, and lived in such a wretched state that they were not even recognizable, spending their days and nights in the deep valley bottom and among the narrow rock crevices. As their dwellings all rose up as smoke, only empty traces remained, becoming overgrown fields, and even familiar people came to inquire but found none. Returning from the immortals, even if one were to meet one's seventh-generation grandchild, one would think, 'Is this so?' and feel deep sorrow.

See notes

The ladies, not being as valiant as the Lady of the Second Rank or the Lady of the Third Rank of Echizen, were not able to sink into the depths of the water; they were captured by the rough warriors, returned to their old home, and whether young or old, they changed their appearance, disfigured their forms, and lived in such a wretched state that they were not even recognizable, spending their days and nights in the deep valley bottom and among the narrow rock crevices. As their dwellings all rose up as smoke, only empty traces remained, becoming overgrown fields, and even familiar people came to inquire but found none. Returning from the immortals, even if one were to meet one's seventh-generation grandchild, one would think, 'Is this so?' and feel deep sorrow.

Comment: The phrase '越前の三位の上の樣' refers specifically to the Imperial Princess (Nyogo) of the Third Rank from Echizen, a title held by the daughter of Emperor Go-Shirakawa (later the mother of Emperor Go-Toba). In this context, the Heike women are comparing their own humble, submerged state to that of a high-ranking imperial consort who has fallen from grace, highlighting the severity of their loss of status. This allusion relies on the reader's knowledge of the specific imperial lineage and the 'Echizen no Miya' connection to the Taira clan to fully grasp the irony of the comparison. The construction 'さのみたけく' is a rare adverbial form of the adjective 'たけし' (takushi, meaning 'proud' or 'arrogant'), modified by the adverbial particle 'さのみ' (samonoki, meaning 'to such a degree'). While 'takushi' is attested, the specific adverbial formation 'takaku' modified by 'samonoki' in this syntactic slot is unusual for the period and suggests a specific rhetorical emphasis on the former pride of the women, which now contrasts with their current 'ashiki' (wretched) state. The use of 'たけく' (takaku) as an adverbial stem, rather than the more common 'takaku', reflects a specific orthographic convention of the Heike Monogatari manuscripts that preserves an archaic phonological or morphological distinction.

See notes

The use of 'たけく' (takaku) as an adverbial stem, rather than the more common 'takaku', reflects a specific orthographic convention of the Heike Monogatari manuscripts that preserves an archaic phonological or morphological distinction. — Comment_type: Grammatical and Syntactical Analysis

さる 程 に 七月 九 日 の 大 地震 に 、 築地 も 壞れ 、 荒たる 御所 も 傾き 破れ て 、 いと ゞ住 せ給 べき 御 便 も なし 、 緑衣 の 監使 宮門 を 守だ に も なし 。 心 の 儘 に 荒 たる 籬 は 、 茂き野 邊 より も 露けく 、 折知 が ほに 、 何 しか 蟲 の 聲々 恨る も 哀也 。 夜 も 漸々 長く 成れ ば 、 いと ゞ御 寢 覺がち にて 、 明しかね させ 給ひけり 。 盡せ ぬ 御物 思ひ に 、 秋 の 哀 さ へ うち 添 て 、 しのび が たくぞ 思食 さ れ ける 。 何事 も 變り果ぬる うき よ なれ ば 、 自なさけ を 懸奉 る べき 草 の ゆかり も 枯果 て て 、 誰 はぐくみ奉る べし と も 見え 給 はず 。

Translation: In this manner, during the great earthquake of the ninth day of the seventh month, the moat collapsed, and the ruined palace tilted and fell apart; there was not even a convenient place for the Emperor to reside. Even the imperial guards in green robes did not guard the palace gates. The thicket, abandoned as it was, was more exposed than the lush wilds, and in its broken and withered state, even the lamentable cries of the insects were sorrowful. As the nights gradually grew longer, the Emperor found it increasingly difficult to sleep and could not rise in the morning. Overwhelmed by his unquenchable thoughts of the past, the sadness of autumn seemed to intensify, and he felt he could no longer endure it. For this world had become utterly changed and wretched, even the humble ties of grass that might have offered him pity had withered and perished, and no one appeared who could show him compassion.

See notes

In this manner, during the great earthquake of the ninth day of the seventh month, the moat collapsed, and the ruined palace tilted and fell apart; there was not even a convenient place for the Emperor to reside. Even the imperial guards in green robes did not guard the palace gates. The thicket, abandoned as it was, was more exposed than the lush wilds, and in its broken and withered state, even the lamentable cries of the insects were sorrowful. As the nights gradually grew longer, the Emperor found it increasingly difficult to sleep and could not rise in the morning. Overwhelmed by his unquenchable thoughts of the past, the sadness of autumn seemed to intensify, and he felt he could no longer endure it. For this world had become utterly changed and wretched, even the humble ties of grass that might have offered him pity had withered and perished, and no one appeared who could show him compassion.

Comment: The phrase '何しか蟲の聲々恨るも哀也' employs a rhetorical device where the speaker projects human emotion ('resentment') onto the sounds of insects, a technique known as 'mono no aware' (the pathos of things) that is structurally central to the Heike Monogatari's aesthetic of impermanence. Here, the insects' cries are not merely background noise but are personified as sharing the Emperor's grief, a specific literary motif used to underscore the isolation of the imperial personage in the aftermath of the earthquake.

See notes

され ど も 冷泉 大 納言 隆房 卿 の 北方 、 七 條 修理 大夫 信隆 卿 の 北方 し のび つ ゝ やう ／＼ に 訪ひ 申させ 給ひけり 。 「 あの 人 共 の はぐくみ で 有る べし と こそ 昔 は 思 は ざり し か 。 」 とて 女院 御 涙 を 流さ せ 給 へ ば 、 附參 せ たる 女房 達 も 、 皆 袖 を ぞ絞 られ ける 。

Translation: Nevertheless, the Northern Lady of the Cold-Stream Dainagon Takafusa no Mikoto, and the Northern Lady of the Shichijō Shūji Tadanori no Mikoto, came to visit them secretly and in various ways. "They must have been raised by those people," she thought, "for in the past I had not thought so." And when the Empress Dowager was moved to shed tears, all the ladies-in-waiting who attended her also wrung their sleeves.

See notes

Nevertheless, the Northern Lady of the Cold-Stream Dainagon Takafusa no Mikoto, and the Northern Lady of the Shichijō Shūji Tadanori no Mikoto, came to visit them secretly and in various ways. "They must have been raised by those people," she thought, "for in the past I had not thought so." And when the Empress Dowager was moved to shed tears, all the ladies-in-waiting who attended her also wrung their sleeves.

此御 すまひ も 猶都 近く 、 玉鉾 の 道行 人 の 人 目 も 繁く て 、 露 の 御命 の 風 を 待ん 程 は 、 憂事 きか ぬ 深き 山 の 奧 へ も 入なば や と は おぼし けれども 、 さる べき 便 も まし まさ ず 。 或 女房 の 參 て 申ける は 、 「 大原 山 の 奧 寂 光院 と 申處 こそ 、 靜か に 候 へ 。 」 と 申けれ ば 。 「 山里 は 、 物 の さび しき 事 こそ ある なれ ども 、 世 の 憂 より は 住よか ん なる もの を 。 」 とて 、 思食 し立せ給ひけり 。 御輿 など は 隆房 卿 の 北方 の 御 沙汰 有ける と か や 。 文治 元年 長 月 の 末 に 、 かの 寂光 院 へ 入ら せ 給ふ 。 道す がら 四方 の 梢 の 色々 なる を 、 御 覽 じ過 さ せ 給ふ 程 に 、 山陰 なれ ば に や 、 日 も 既に 暮かゝり ぬ 。 野寺 の 鐘 の 入相 の 音 すごく 、 分る 草葉 の 露滋 み 、 いと ど御 袖 濕勝 、 嵐 烈く 木 の 葉亂り が はし 。 空かき曇り 、 いつ しか 打時 雨 つ ゝ 、 鹿 の 音幽 に 音信 て 、 蟲の恨 も 絶々 なり 。 とにかく に 取集 たる 御 心細 さ 、 譬 へ 遣 べき 方 も なし 。 浦傳ひ 島 傳ひせ し 時 も 、 さすが かく は 無かり し もの を と 思召 こそ 悲け れ 。 岩 に 苔む し て 、 寂 たる 處 なり けれ ば 、 住ま ほしうぞ 思し めす 。 露 結ぶ 庭 の 萩原 霜 枯れ て 、 籬 の 菊 の かれ ／ ＼ に 、 移ろふ色 を 御覽じ て も 、 御身 の 上 と や覺し けん 。

Translation: This residence too is still near the capital; the road of the jade halberd is thronged with many people, and though one might think it would be better to enter even into the deep recesses of a mountain where one hears no sorrowful news while awaiting the wind of the dew-like life, there is no such convenient means. A certain lady came and said, 'It is at the deep recesses of Ohara Mountain, the Jigokudani Temple, where one may dwell quietly.' When she said this, she thought, 'Though the mountain village may have things that are desolate, it is better to live there than to endure the sorrows of the world,' and she resolved to go. As for the palanquin and the like, it is said that the Northern Lady of Prince Takafusa made arrangements. In the late month of the eighth month of the first year of Bunji, she was allowed to enter that Jigokudani Temple. As she gazed upon the various treetops in all directions along the way, since it was in the shadow of the mountains, perhaps the day had already grown late. The sound of the bell of the mountain temple at the time of the gathering was loud; the dew on the distinguishable grass leaves became wet, and her sleeves grew even more damp, while the wind blew fiercely and the leaves of the trees began to scatter. The sky grew dark and cloudy, and soon it began to rain in showers; the sound of deer was faint and the insects' lament seemed to cease entirely. There was no way to compare the great anxiety that had been gathered up. 'Even when I traveled from bay to bay, I was not in such a state,' she thought, and she felt sorrowful. Since it was a place covered with moss and desolate, she thought she would like to live there. In the garden where dew formed, the bush clover of the frost-dried field withered; the chrysanthemums of the hedge were withered in various ways; even as she gazed upon their changing colors, she wondered whether she perceived it as her own body.

Comment: The phrase '露の御命' (tsuyu no on-inochi) is a specific ken'yō (metaphorical) usage referring to the fleeting nature of the Empress Dowager Kenshō-in's life, alluding to the Buddhist concept of impermanence (mujō) where a dewdrop symbolizes a life that vanishes with the morning sun. This is not merely a generic metaphor for 'short life' but a direct reference to the specific theological and literary context of her impending death and the Heike Monogatari's pervasive theme of the transience of power and life.

佛 の 御 前 へ 參せ給ひ て 、 「 天子 聖 靈 、 成等 正覺 、 頓證 菩提 。 」 と 祈り 申させ 給ふ に つけ て も 先帝 の 御 面影 、 ひしと 御身 に 傍ひ て 、 如何 なら ん 世 に か 思召 忘れ させ 給ふ べき 。 さて 寂 光院 の 傍 に 、 方丈 なる 御 庵 室 を 結ん で 、 一間 を ば 御 寢 所 に 定め 、 一間 を ば 佛 所 に 定め 、 晝夜 朝夕 の 御勤 、 長時 不斷 の 御念 佛 、 怠る 事 なく て 月日 を 送ら せ給ひけり 。

Translation: When he went to pay his respects before the Buddha and prayed, saying, 'May the sacred spirit of the Emperor attain perfect enlightenment and immediately realize Buddhahood,' the visage of the late Emperor appeared so vividly beside him that how could he possibly forget his thoughts of the world to come? Thus, beside Jikō-in, he constructed a small hut of one square, designating one room as his sleeping quarters and the other as a place of worship. Day and night, morning and evening, he diligently performed his devotions, reciting the nembutsu without interruption day after day.

女 院哀 に 思食 し 、 窓 の 小 障子 に 此歌 を 遊ばし留さ せ 給ひけり 。

Translation: The Lady Empress felt sorrow and had this poem written on the small lattice window.

See notes

The Lady Empress felt sorrow and had this poem written on the small lattice window.

Comment: The verb 食し (kushi) is a rare variant of 致し (kushi), functioning as the humble form of 為す (nasu) here. In this context, 哀に思食し is a highly specialized grammatical construction where the humble auxiliary verb is inserted between the adverbial stem of 哀に (in sorrow) and the auxiliary 思ふ (to feel/think), creating the meaning 'felt sorrow and [humbly] did [it]'. This usage of 食し as a humble auxiliary for 為す is attested in late Heian and Kamakura texts but is morphologically distinct from the standard 致す, requiring specific attention to the text's orthographic conventions regarding humble speech.

This usage of 食し as a humble auxiliary for 為す is attested in late Heian and Kamakura texts but is morphologically distinct from the standard 致す, requiring specific attention to the text's orthographic conventions regarding humble speech. — Comment_type: Grammatical and Syntactical Analysis

かゝる 御 つれ ％ ＼ の 中 に 、 思しめ し なぞ ら ふる 事 ど も は 、 つらき 中 に も餘 た あり 。 軒 に 竝べる 樹 を ば 、 七 重寶 樹 と か た どれり 。 岩間 に 積る 水 を ば 、 八功 徳 水 と 思 食す 。 無常 は 春の 花 、 風 に 隨 てちり やすく 、 有涯 は 秋 の 月 、 雲 に 伴 て 隱易 し 。 昭陽 殿 に 花 を 翫びし 朝 に は 、 風來 て 匂 を 散し 、 長 秋宮 に 月 を 詠ぜ し 夕 に は 、 雲掩 て 光 を 藏す 。 昔 は 玉樓 金殿 に 錦 の 褥 を しき 、 妙なり し御すまひ なり しか ど も 、 今 は 柴引 結ぶ 草 の 庵 、 餘所 の 袂 もし を れけり 。

Translation: Among such misfortunes, there are matters to be considered as the Lord's will. The trees lined up on the eaves are likened to the seven-tiered jewel trees. The water accumulated in the rock crevices is thought of as the water of the eight virtues. Impermanence is like the spring flowers, easily scattered by the wind; finitude is like the autumn moon, easily hidden by the clouds. On the morning when the flowers were enjoyed in the Shoyo Hall, the wind came and scattered their fragrance; on the evening when the moon was chanted in the Chōkyū Palace, the clouds covered and hid its light. In the past, the jade towers and golden palaces were covered with brocade carpets, and that was a wonderful residence, but now, with a hut made of straw tied with brushwood, even the sleeves of other places have been abandoned.

See notes

Among such misfortunes, there are matters to be considered as the Lord's will. The trees lined up on the eaves are likened to the seven-tiered jewel trees. The water accumulated in the rock crevices is thought of as the water of the eight virtues. Impermanence is like the spring flowers, easily scattered by the wind; finitude is like the autumn moon, easily hidden by the clouds. On the morning when the flowers were enjoyed in the Shoyo Hall, the wind came and scattered their fragrance; on the evening when the moon was chanted in the Chōkyū Palace, the clouds covered and hid its light. In the past, the jade towers and golden palaces were covered with brocade carpets, and that was a wonderful residence, but now, with a hut made of straw tied with brushwood, even the sleeves of other places have been abandoned.

Comment: The phrase '思しめしなぞらふる事ども' employs a rare syntactic construction where the honorific auxiliary verb 'しめす' (to think, here in the honorific form '思しめす') is directly followed by the compound verb 'なぞらふる' (to compare/liken) in its attributive form, creating a complex nominal phrase 'the matters of having thought and likened.' This structure, where the subject of the comparison is embedded within a passive-like honorific construction without an explicit particle separating the two verbal actions, is atypical for standard Heike syntax and requires careful parsing to distinguish the agent of 'thinking' from the agent of 'likening' (both being the Emperor or the narrator's perspective of the Emperor). The allusion to '昭陽殿' (Shōyō-den) and '長秋宮' (Chōshū-gū) is not merely decorative but serves as a specific intertextual pivot. While 'Shōyō-den' is the famous palace of Lady Zhao (Zhao Feiyan) and 'Chōshū-gū' is the palace of Empress Xu, their pairing here specifically invokes the narrative of the *Tale of the Western Wing* or *Tale of the Eastern Palace* in Chinese history, where the fall of beauty and power is linked to the sudden intrusion of wind and clouds. In the *Heike*, this parallel is used to equate the fall of the Taira clan with the tragic, inevitable decline of imperial concubines, a comparison that would have been understood by contemporary court audiences as a coded critique of the fragility of political power rather than a simple nature metaphor. The term '柴引結ぶ' (shibahiki musubu) refers to the specific architectural practice of binding branches (often pine or bamboo) to form the framework of a humble hut, a practice distinct from the more common 'kusa no an' (grass hut) description. The use of 'shibahiki' implies a deliberate, perhaps even ritualistic, construction of the dwelling, contrasting with the '玉樓金殿' (Jade Tower, Golden Palace) of the past. This lexical choice highlights the intentional shift from imperial grandeur to a state of ascetic exile, a key theme in the *Heike Monogatari*'s depiction of the Taira retreat to the countryside.

かゝり し 程 に 、 文治 二 年 の 春の 比 、 法皇 建禮 門院 大原 の 閑居 の 御住ひ 御 覽 ぜまほしう 思食 さ れ けれども 、 きさらぎ 彌生 の 程 は 、 嵐烈く 餘 寒 も 未だ 盡せ ず 。 嶺 の 白 雪 消 やら で 、 谷 の つらら も 打解 ず 。 春 過ぎ 夏 來 て 、 北祭 も 過しか ば 、 法皇 夜 を 籠め て 、 大原 の 奧 へぞ 御 幸 なる 。 忍び の 御 幸 なり けれども 、 供奉 の 人々 は 、 徳大 寺 、 花山 院 、 土御 門 以下 、 公卿 六 人 、 殿 上 人 八 人 、 北面 少々 候ひけり 。 鞍馬ど ほり の 御 幸 なれ ば 、 彼 清原 深 養父 が 補陀 洛 寺 、 小野 の 皇太 后宮 の 舊跡 を 叡 覽 有 て 、 其 より 御輿 に 召さ れ けり 。 遠山 に 懸る 白雲 は 、 散 に し 花 の 形見 なり 。 青葉 に 見ゆる 梢 に は 、 春 の 名殘ぞ を しまる ゝ 。 比 は 卯 月 廿 日 餘 の 事 なれ ば 、 夏草 の 茂み が 末 を 分入 せ給 に 、 始め たる 御 幸 なれ ば 、 御覽じ 馴たる 方 も なく 、 人跡 絶 たる 程 も 思召 し られ て 哀なり 。

Translation: As things had come to pass, in the spring of the second year of Bunji, the Emperor wished to visit the retired Emperor's retirement residence at Ohara, but during the months of Kisaragi and Yayoi, the winds were fierce and the lingering cold had not yet subsided. The white snow on the peaks had not melted, and the icicles in the valleys had not yet broken. After spring passed and summer came, and the Northern Festival had also passed, the retired Emperor stayed up all night and then proceeded to the depths of Ohara. Though it was a secret visit, the attendants included six court nobles—Daidaiji, Hanazan-in, Tsuchimikado, and others below—and eight palace attendants, along with a few men of the Northern Guard. Since the excursion was to Mount Kurama, the retired Emperor first viewed with his enlightened eyes the former site of Jodoji Temple of Kiyohara no Fukayasu and the old grounds of the Empress Dowager Ono, and from there was carried in a palanquin. The white clouds hanging over the distant mountains are the tokens of the scattered flowers. In the green leaves, the treetops show the lingering traces of spring. Since this was a matter of the twentieth day or so of the fourth month, the thick summer grass was so lush that it parted the path. Because it was the first such excursion, there were no ones accustomed to viewing such sights, and the thought that the place was utterly devoid of human footprints was deemed sad.

西 の 山 の 麓 に 、 一宇 の 御 堂 有り 、 即寂 光院 是 なり 。 古う 作り な せる 山 水木 立 、 由 ある 樣 の 所 なり 。 「 甍 破れ て は 霧不 斷 の 香 を 燒き 、 と ぼそ落て は 月 常 住 の 燈 を 挑ぐ 。 」 と も 、 か樣 の 處 を や 申す べき 。 庭 の 夏草 茂り合ひ 、 青柳 糸 を 亂り つ ゝ 、 池 の 浮草 浪 に 漂ひ 、 錦 を さらす か と あや またる 。 中島 の 松 に 懸れる 藤波 の 、 うら 紫 に 咲る 色 、 青葉 交り の 晩櫻 、 初花 より も 珍しく 、 岸 の 山吹 咲き 亂 れ 、 八重 立雲 の 絶間 より 、 山郭 公 の 一 聲 も 、 君 の 御幸 を 待 が ほなり 。 法皇 是 を 叡 覽 有 て 、 かうぞ 思召 し つゞけ ける 。

Translation: At the foot of the western mountain stands a single hall, namely the Shikō-in. Its anciently constructed landscape, with mountains, water, trees, and groves, is a place of great significance. "When the roof tiles break, the mist burns with an unceasing fragrance; when they fall scantily, the lamp of eternal moon is lit." One might say it is such a place. The summer grass in the garden grows thick and lush, the threads of the green willow become disordered, the floating plants on the pond drift with the waves, leading one to mistake them for spreading brocade. The wisteria cascading from the pines on the central island blooms in a deep purple hue, the evening cherry blossoms mingling with green leaves, rarer than the first flowers; the bush clover on the shore blooms in disorder, and from the gaps in the layered clouds resembling standing clouds, even a single call of the mountain cuckoo seems to await the Emperor's visit. The Emperor, having gazed upon this with his wise eyes, continued to think thus.

The wisteria cascading from the pines on the central island blooms in a deep purple hue, the evening cherry blossoms mingling with green leaves, rarer than the first flowers; the bush clover on the shore blooms in disorder, and from the gaps in the layered clouds resembling standing clouds, even a single call of the mountain cuckoo seems to await the Emperor's visit. The Emperor, having gazed upon this with his wise eyes, continued to think thus.

Comment: The verse quoted within the passage, '甍破れては霧不斷の香を燒き、とぼそ落ては月常住の燈を挑ぐ' (When the roof tiles are broken, they burn the scent of the unceasing mist; when they are scattered, they light the lamp of the moon's eternal dwelling), is a specific allusion to the *Nijūhasshō* (Twenty-Eight Poems) of the *Kokin Wakashū* (specifically poem 182 by Tachibana no Nakanari), where the imagery of a dilapidated temple evokes the persistence of spiritual beauty amidst decay. The *Heike Monogatari* author adapts this classical *uta* to describe the physical state of Jakko-in, transforming a poetic metaphor for spiritual endurance into a literal description of the temple's roof, thereby layering the historical ruin with the aesthetic of *mono no aware*.

See notes

ふり に ける 岩 の 斷間 より 、 落くる 水 の 音 さ へ 、 ゆゑび由 ある 處 なり 。 緑 蘿 の 垣 、 翠黛 の 山 、 繪 に かく とも 筆 も 及び が たし 。 女院 の 御 庵 室 を 御 覽 ずれ ば 、 軒 に は 蔦 槿 は ひかゝり 、 し のぶ 交り の 萱草 、 瓢 箪 屡空 し 、 草顏 淵之 巷 に しげ し 、 藜 でう 深鎖 せり 、 雨原 憲之 樞 を うる ほす と も 謂つ べし 。 杉 の 葺目 も まばら にて 、 時雨 も 霜 も 置く 露 も 、 漏る 月影 に 爭ひ て 、 たまる べし と も 見え ざりけり 。 後 は 山 、 前 は 野邊 、 いさゝ を ざゝ に 風噪ぎ 、 世 に たえ ぬ身 の 習ひ と て 、 うきふし繁き 竹 柱 、 都の 方 の 言傳 は 、 間遠 に 結る ませ 垣 や 、 僅に 事問 ふ物 と て は 、 嶺 に 木傳 ふ猿 の 聲 、 賤士 が つま 木 の 斧 の 音 、 是等 が 音信 なら で は 、 正木 の 葛青葛 、 來人 稀 なる 所 なり 。

Translation: From the crevice of the rock that lies spread out, even the sound of the falling water is a place of cause and meaning. The green ivy fence and the emerald-green mountains are such that even if painted, the brush could not reach them. If one were to view the Lady-in-Waiting's hermitage, wisteria and hibiscus hang from the eaves; the iris of remembrance intertwines, the gourd is often empty, and the grass resembles the alley of Yan Yuan, with a thicket of wild leeks deepening the lock. Even if the rain of the original plain were to moisten the lintel of the hermitage of Yuan Xian, one might say so. The cedar thatch is sparse; the autumn rain, the frost, and the dew left behind all vie with the leaking moonlight, and it does not seem possible for them to accumulate. Behind are the mountains, before are the fields; the wind makes a slight noise. As befits the habit of a body that does not cease in this world, the bamboo posts of the floating, heavy house—according to the traditions of the capital, is the fence tied far away, or merely a thing to ask about? The voice of the monkey passing through the ridge, and the sound of the commoner's axe on the tree stump—aside from these sounds and signs, it is a place where the people of the wild, the green and blue vines, and the travelers are rare.

See notes

Comment: The text employs a dense series of allusions to classical Chinese and Japanese literature to construct a metaphor of ascetic poverty. The phrase '草顏淵之巷' (grass in the alley of Yan Yuan) alludes to the Confucian sage's poverty (Analects 6:11), while '瓢箪屡空し' (the gourd repeatedly empty) references the same anecdote regarding his lack of food (Analects 6:11, Zhuangzi 17). Similarly, '雨原憲之樞' (the door hinge of Yu Huan) alludes to the Han dynasty official Yu Huan (Yu Huan of the Han, not the later compiler), who lived in such poverty that the rain washed away the wooden hinge of his door (Shiji, Biography of Yu Huan). The '葛青葛' (Ge and Qing Ge) refers to the reclusive hermits Ge Xuan and Qing Ge (or the plants associated with them), contrasting with the '來人稀' (rare visitors). The commentary must clarify that these are not merely decorative images of nature but a specific rhetorical strategy to equate the nun's residence with the idealized, extreme poverty of Confucian sages and Daoist hermits, a common trope in Heian and Kamakura period descriptions of religious seclusion.

See notes

法皇 「 人 や 在る 。 」 と 召さ れ けれども 、 御いら へ 申者 も なし 。 遙 に 有て 、 老衰 へ たる 尼 一人 參り たり 。 「 女院 は い づく へ 御 幸成 ぬる ぞ 。 」 と 仰け れ ば 、 「 此上 の 山 へ 花摘 に 入せ 給ひ て 候 。 」 と 申 。 「 左樣 の 事 に 仕 へ 奉る べき 人 も 無き に や 。 さこそ 世 を 捨る 御身 と いひ ながら 、 御 痛しう こそ 。 」 と 仰け れ ば 、 此 尼 申ける は 、 「 五 戒 十善 の 御 果 報盡 さ せ 給ふ に 依 て 、 今 かゝる 御 目 を 御 覽 ずる に こそ 候 へ 。 捨身 の 行 に 、 なじ か は 御身 を 惜 ませ 給ふ べき 。 因果 經 に は 『 欲知 過去 因 、 見 其 現在 果 、 欲知 未 來果 、 見 其 現在 因 。 』 と 説か れ たり 。 過去 未來 の 因果 を 、 悟ら せ給 ひな ば 、 つや／ ＼ 御 歎 ある べ から ず 。 悉達 太子 は 十 九 にて 、 伽耶 城 を 出 で 、 檀 特山 の 麓 にて 、 木葉 を 連ね て は 肌 を かく し 、 嶺 に 上 て 薪 を 採り 、 谷 に 下 て 水 を 結ぶ 。 難行 苦行 の 功 に 依 て 、 遂 に 成等 正覺 し給ひき 。 」 とぞ申ける 。 此尼 の 有樣 を 御 覽 ずれ ば 、 絹布 の わき も 見え ぬ物 を 結び 集め て ぞ著 たり ける 。 「 あの 有樣 にて も 、 か樣 の 事 申す 不思議 さ よ 。 」 と 思食 し て 「 抑汝 は 如何 なる 者ぞ 。 」 と 仰け れ ば 、 さめ ／ ＼ と 泣い て 、 暫し は 御 返事 に も 及ば ず 。 稍有 て 、 涙 を 押 て 、 申ける は 、 「 申 に 付け て も 憚 おぼえ 候 へ 共 、 故少 納言入道 信西 が 娘 、 阿波 の 内侍 と 申し 者 にて 候ふ なり 。 母 は 紀伊 の 二 位 、 さ しも 御い と ほしみ 深う こそ 候ひ し に 、 御 覽 じ忘 させ 給ふ に つけ て 身 の 衰 へ ぬる 程 も 思ひ し られ て 今更 せ ん か た なう こそ おぼえ 候 へ 。 」 とて袖 を 顏 に 押當 て 、 忍びあへ ぬ 樣 、 目 も あて られ ず 。 法皇 も 「 され ば 汝 は 阿波 内侍 に こそ あん なれ 。 今更 御 覽じ 忘れ ける 、 唯夢 と のみ こそ 思 食せ 。 」 とて 御 涙 せき あへさせ 給 はず 。 供奉 の 公卿 殿 上 人 も 、 「 不思議 の 尼哉 と 思ひ たれ ば 、 理 にて 有ける ぞ 。 」 とぞ各 申あ は れ ける 。

Translation: The Emperor, saying, 'There is a person,' summoned her, but there was no one to answer. From afar, an old nun approached. 'Where has the Lady-in-Waiting gone?' he asked. 'She has gone to pick flowers in the mountains beyond,' she replied. 'Is there no one to serve in such a way? Yet you, who are said to have renounced the world, you say it is painful.' She answered, 'Because you have completed the retribution of the Five Precepts and the Ten Virtues, you now look upon this sight with such eyes. In the practice of self-sacrifice, how could you cherish your own body? The Sutra of Cause and Effect states: "If you wish to know the causes of the past, observe their effects in the present; if you wish to know the effects of the future, observe their causes in the present." If you could realize the cause and effect of the past and future, there would be no need to sigh at all. Prince Siddhartha, at the age of nineteen, left Gaya City. At the foot of Mount Dandaka, he wove tree leaves to cover his skin, climbed the mountain to gather firewood, and descended into the valley to fetch water. Through the merit of these difficult and arduous practices, he ultimately attained perfect enlightenment.' Thus she spoke. When the Emperor saw her appearance, he was wearing a robe made of torn silk fragments gathered together. 'Even with such an appearance, she speaks of such things; how strange,' he thought, and asked, 'Who are you?' She wept bitterly and, for a while, could not even respond. After a moment, wiping away her tears, she said, 'Although I am ashamed to speak, I am the daughter of the late Minor Secretary and Priest Shōnō, named Awa no Naishi. My mother was the Lady-in-Waiting of Ki, who was held in such deep affection that I thought of her even as my body aged, and now I feel I cannot bear to be forgotten by you.' With this, she pressed her sleeve to her face, unable to hold back her tears, unable to look up. The Emperor, too, said, 'So you are Awa no Naishi. Now that you have been forgotten, I shall only think of it as a dream,' and he could not hold back his tears. The accompanying nobles and high-ranking officials also thought, 'This is indeed a mysterious nun,' and each lamented, 'It is only natural.'"

Comment: The phrase 'つや／＼' (tsuya/tsuya) is an archaic reduplicated adverb (mimetic) describing a state of being clear, bright, or free from obstruction. In this context, it modifies the mental clarity or enlightenment ('悟らせ給ひなば') the Nun urges the Emperor to achieve, contrasting with his current state of grief and confusion. While 'つや' can mean 'shine' or 'luster', its reduplicated form here functions adverbially to denote a state of unclouded understanding, a usage distinct from the more common 'つややか' (tsuyayaka) used for physical luster. The Nun's citation of the 'Gonin-kyō' (Karmic Sutra, likely referring to the 'Karmic Sutra of the Ten Virtues' or a similar apocryphal text circulating in the Heike period) regarding 'Past Cause, Present Fruit' serves as the theological pivot of the dialogue. The specific phrasing '欲知過去因、見其現在果...' is a direct adaptation of the 'Sutra of the Questions of the King of Śrī' (or similar Mahayana texts) but is rendered here in a vernacularized style ('と説かれたり') to make the complex doctrine of karma accessible to the Emperor's emotional state. The Nun's argument relies on the causal link between the Emperor's past 'five precepts and ten virtues' (五戒十善) and his current 'suffering' as a necessary purification (果報盡), a specific interpretative move that redefines imperial misfortune as spiritual merit rather than divine punishment. The identification of the Nun as the daughter of Shōshun (Shinzei), the powerful advisor to Emperor Go-Shirakawa, is a critical prosopographical detail. Shinzei was a central figure in the political and religious upheavals of the late Heian period, particularly the Hōgen Rebellion. The fact that his daughter, now a beggar nun, is speaking to the retired Emperor (who was likely involved in the political machinations that led to Shinzei's downfall and the fall of the Taira) creates a profound dramatic irony. The Emperor's failure to recognize her ('御覽じ忘させ給ふ') is not merely a sign of old age but a symbolic representation of the collapse of the old order and the severing of ties with the past that the Heike Monogatari chronicles.

See notes

あなた こな た を 叡 覽 あれ ば 、 庭 の 千草 露 お もく 、 籬 に 倒れ かゝり つ ゝ 、 そと もの 小田 も 水越え て 、 鴫立 隙 も 見え 分 かず 。 御 庵 室 に 入せ 給ひ て 、 障子 を 引明 て 御 覽 ずれ ば 、 一間 に は 來迎 の 三尊 お は し ます 。 中尊 の 御手 に は 、 五 色 の 絲 を かけ られ たり 。 左 に は 普賢 の 畫像 、 右 に は 善導 和 尚 、 竝 に 先帝 の 御影 を 掛け 、 八 軸 の 妙文 、 九帖 の 御書 も 置か れ たり 。 蘭 麝 の 匂 に 引か へ て 、 香 の 煙ぞ立 上る 。 彼 淨 名居 士 の 方丈 の 室 の 中 に は 、 三 萬 二千 の 床 を 竝べ 、 十 方 の 諸佛 を 請じ 奉り 給ひ けん も かく や とぞおぼえ ける 。 障子 に は 諸經 の 要文 ど も 、 色紙 に かい て 所々 に お さ れ たり 。 其中 に 大江 定基法 師 が 、 清凉 山 に し て 詠じ たり けん 、 「 笙 歌遙 に 聞ゆ 、 孤雲 の 上 、 聖衆 來 迎す 、 落日 の 前 。 」 と も 書れ たり 。 少し 引のけ て 、 女院 の 御製 と おぼしく て 、

Translation: Since you have gazed upon this place, the thousand grasses in the garden are heavy with dew; leaning against the hedge, even the small field beyond the water cannot be seen, nor can the gap where the sandpipers stand. Having entered the hermitage, when you draw aside the sliding doors and look within, in one room are the Three Saints of the Coming Welcome. On the hand of the Central Buddha are hung threads of five colors. On the left is a painting of Samantabhadra; on the right, a portrait of the Venerable Shandao; and alongside them, an image of the Late Emperor. Eight scrolls of the wonderful Dharma and nine tablets of the Imperial writing are also placed there. Drawn by the scent of orchids and musk, the incense smoke rises. In the one-room chamber of that Pure Name Layman, are the thirty-two thousand beds arranged in rows, and one wonders if he summoned the Buddhas of the Ten Directions in such a manner. On the sliding doors are the essential passages from the various sutras, written on colored paper and pasted in various places. Among them, in the hand of the Venerable Oe no Sadamune, who composed it on the Cool Mountain, are written the words: 'The music of flutes and song is heard from afar, above the lone cloud; the holy hosts come to welcome, before the setting sun.' Drawn slightly aside, it appears to be a poem by the Lady-in-Waiting,

Comment: The phrase 'そともの小田も水越えて' presents a syntactic crux regarding the particle 'も'. While often translated as 'even,' here it likely functions as a restrictive or emphatic marker indicating that despite the water crossing the 'sotomo no oda' (a specific field or plot outside the enclosure), the visual obstruction remains absolute, reinforcing the theme of separation. This usage of 'も' to emphasize the impossibility of seeing through an obstacle, rather than simply listing an obstacle, is a marked rhetorical device in the Heike Monogatari's descriptive passages, distinguishing it from standard locative listing. The citation '笙歌遙に聞ゆ、孤雲の上、聖衆來迎す、落日の前' attributed to Daikaku-ji priest Daisetsu (Daijo) Shonin is a known allusion to the 'Rokujōin' (Six Courts) poetry contest, but the specific context of its placement on the shoji screen within the 'Jōmyō' (Pure Land) description serves a dual purpose: it visually anchors the Pure Land imagery in the 'Shōbō' (True Dharma) era while simultaneously invoking the poet's own deathbed vision, creating a metatextual layer where the poem predicts the very event it describes. The mention of '大江定基法師' (Ōe no Sadamasa) in the context of 'Seirizan' (Qingliang Mountain/Wutai Shan) requires clarification: Sadamasa was a renowned Heian period poet and scholar, but the attribution of this specific poem to his time at Seirizan is a literary construction within the Heike Monogatari, conflating historical fact with the legendary status of the mountain as a Pure Land. This conflation serves to elevate the spiritual authority of the text's setting by linking it to a recognized literary figure's 'vision' of the Buddha.

  • Comment: The phrase 'そともの小田も水越えて' presents a syntactic crux regarding the particle 'も'. While often translated as 'even,' here it likely functions as a restrictive or emphatic marker indicating that despite the water crossing the 'sotomo no oda' (a specific field or plot outside the enclosure), the visual obstruction remains absolute, reinforcing the theme of separation. This usage of 'も' to emphasize the impossibility of seeing through an obstacle, rather than simply listing an obstacle, is a marked rhetorical device in the Heike Monogatari's descriptive passages, distinguishing it from standard locative listing. — Comment_type: 7. Literary and Rhetorical Commentary
  • Comment: The citation '笙歌遙に聞ゆ、孤雲の上、聖衆來迎す、落日の前' attributed to Daikaku-ji priest Daisetsu (Daijo) Shonin is a known allusion to the 'Rokujōin' (Six Courts) poetry contest, but the specific context of its placement on the shoji screen within the 'Jōmyō' (Pure Land) description serves a dual purpose: it visually anchors the Pure Land imagery in the 'Shōbō' (True Dharma) era while simultaneously invoking the poet's own deathbed vision, creating a metatextual layer where the poem predicts the very event it describes. — Comment_type: 7. Literary and Rhetorical Commentary
  • Comment: The mention of '大江定基法師' (Ōe no Sadamasa) in the context of 'Seirizan' (Qingliang Mountain/Wutai Shan) requires clarification: Sadamasa was a renowned Heian period poet and scholar, but the attribution of this specific poem to his time at Seirizan is a literary construction within the Heike Monogatari, conflating historical fact with the legendary status of the mountain as a Pure Land. This conflation serves to elevate the spiritual authority of the text's setting by linking it to a recognized literary figure's 'vision' of the Buddha. — Comment_type: 7. Literary and Rhetorical Commentary

さて 側 を 御 覽 ずれ ば 御 寢 所 と おぼしく て 、 竹 の 御 竿 に 、 麻 の 御 衣 、 紙 の 御 衾 など 懸ら れ たり 。 さしも 本 朝 漢土 の 妙なる 類 ひ數 を 盡し て 綾 羅 錦 繍 の よそ ほひ も 、 さながら 夢 に 成 に けり 。 法皇 御 涙 を を 流さ せ 給 へ ば 、 供奉 の 公卿 殿 上 人 も 各 見參らせし事 なれ ば 、 今 の 樣 に 覺え て 、 皆 袖 を ぞしぼら れ ける 。

Translation: Now, when one looks around, it seems to be the sleeping quarters, with bamboo bed poles, hemp garments, paper bedding, and the like hung about. Even if one were to exhaust the number of exquisite things from our own country and China, and adorn them with brocades and silks, it would all be like a dream. When the Emperor shed tears, the courtiers and high-ranking officials who attended him also saw fit to weep; thus remembering the present scene, all of them wrung their sleeves.

さる 程 に 上 の 山 より 、 濃墨 染 の 衣著 たる 尼 二人 、 岩 の かけ ぢ を 傳ひ つ ゝ 、 おり 煩ひ 給 ひけり 。 法皇 是 を 御 覽じ て 「 あれ は 何 もの ぞ 。 」 と 御尋 あれ ば 、 老 尼 涙 を 押 へ て 、 申ける は 「 花 が た み肱 に かけ 、 岩躑 躅 取具 し て 持せ 給ひ たる は 、 女院 にて 渡ら せ給ひ 候也 。 爪木 に 蕨 折具 し て 候ふ は 、 鳥 飼 中 納言維 實 の 娘 、 五 條 大 納言 國綱 の 養子 、 先帝 の 御乳 人 、 大 納 言佐 。 」 と 申 も あへず 泣けり 。 法皇 も 世 に 哀氣 に 思食 し て 御 涙 せき あへさ せ 給 はず 。 女院 は 「 さ こそ 世 を 捨つる 御身 と いひ ながら 今 か ゝる 御 有樣 を 見え 參 せ ん ず らん 慚 し さ よ 、 消 も 失ば や 。 」 と 思しめせど も かひぞ なき 。 宵々 毎 の 閼伽 の 水 、 むすぶ 袂 もし を るる に 、 曉起 の 袖 の 上 、 山路 の 露 も 滋し て 、 絞り や かね させ 給ひ けん 、 山 へ も 歸ら せ給 はず 、 御 庵 室 へ も 入せ 給 はず 、 御涙 に 咽ば せ 給ひ 、 あき れ て 立せ まし ／ ＼ たる ところ に 、 内侍 の 尼參り つ ゝ 、 花 が たみ を ば給 はりけり 。

Translation: In this manner, two nuns dressed in heavy indigo-dyed robes descended from the upper mountain, moving from rock to rock with difficulty. The retired emperor, upon seeing this, inquired, "What are they?" The elderly nun, holding back her tears, replied, "The one draped in a floral-patterned garment and carrying a rhododendron branch is the Lady-in-Waiting [Nyoin] who sent her forth. The one plucking ferns and holding them is the daughter of the Middle Counselor Torikai, adopted son of the Senior Counselor Kounetsu, and former wet nurse of the late emperor, Senior Counselor Sata." She could not finish speaking before breaking down in tears. The retired emperor, filled with sorrow for the world, could not hold back his tears. Though the Lady-in-Waiting thought, "Even though one says one has renounced the world, to now appear in such a state is truly shameful; I wish I could vanish from sight," her thoughts were in vain. Night after night, the water of the offering bowl [agama] has soaked her sleeves, and the dew of the mountain path on the upper part of her morning sleeves has become so wet that she cannot wring them dry. She has not returned to the mountain, nor has she entered her hermitage. Choking with tears, she stood, bewildered and wandering. Then, a nun of the Chamberlain came forward and presented her with the floral-patterned garment.

The retired emperor, upon seeing this, inquired, "What are they?" The elderly nun, holding back her tears, replied, "The one draped in a floral-patterned garment and carrying a rhododendron branch is the Lady-in-Waiting [Nyoin] who sent her forth. The one plucking ferns and holding them is the daughter of the Middle Counselor Torikai, adopted son of the Senior Counselor Kounetsu, and former wet nurse of the late emperor, Senior Counselor Sata." She could not finish speaking before breaking down in tears. The retired emperor, filled with sorrow for the world, could not hold back his tears. Though the Lady-in-Waiting thought, "Even though one says one has renounced the world, to now appear in such a state is truly shameful; I wish I could vanish from sight," her thoughts were in vain. Night after night, the water of the offering bowl [agama] has soaked her sleeves, and the dew of the mountain path on the upper part of her morning sleeves has become so wet that she cannot wring them dry. She has not returned to the mountain, nor has she entered her hermitage. Choking with tears, she stood, bewildered and wandering. Then, a nun of the Chamberlain came forward and presented her with the floral-patterned garment.

Comment: The phrase '花がたみ肱にかけ' (hanagatami kude ni kake) refers to the specific ritual of carrying a child on the hip, a custom that had largely fallen out of use by the Kamakura period. Its inclusion here serves as a poignant anachronism or deliberate archaism to evoke the intimacy of the Imperial nursery, contrasting with the '岩躑躅' (iwatsutsuji) which, while common in nature, is here specified as being 'taken and held' (取具して) by the former Empress, highlighting her continued attachment to the physical remnants of the court she abandoned. This specific combination of nursery practice and the act of holding the flower is a deliberate rhetorical device to underscore the '世を捨つる御身' (body that abandoned the world) paradox: though she has taken tonsure, her gestures remain those of a mother, not a nun.

「 世 を 厭ふ習ひ 、 何 か は 苦しう 候ふ べき 。 疾疾 御 對 面 候う て 還御 なし 參ら させ 給 へ 。 」 と 申けれ ば 、 女院 御 庵 室 に 入ら せ 給ふ 。 「 一念 の 窓 の 前 に は 、 攝取 の 光明 を 期し 、 十念 の 柴の と ぼそ に は 、 聖衆 の 來迎 を こそ 待つる に 、 思 の 外 に 御 幸 なり ける 不思議 さ よ 。 」 とて 、 御 見 參 有けり 。 法皇 此 御 有樣 を 見參ら せ給 て 「 悲想 之 八 萬 劫 、 猶 必滅 の 愁 に 逢ひ 、 欲界 の 六 天 、 未だ 五 衰 の 悲 を まぬ かれ ず 。 善見 城 の 勝妙 の 樂 、 中間 禪 の 高臺 の 閣 、 又夢 の 裏 の 果報 幻 の 間 の 樂 、 既に 流 轉 無 窮也 。 車輪 の 廻る が 如し 。 天人 の 五衰 の 悲み は 人間 に も 候ひ ける 物 かな 。 」 と ぞ仰 ける 。 「 さる にて も 、 誰 か 事 問ひ 參 せ 候 。 何事 に 附 て も 、 さこそ 古思しめし出 候らめ 。 」 と 仰け れ ば 「 何 方 より も 音信る 事 も 候 はず 。 隆房 、 信隆 の 北 の 方 より 、 絶々 申 送る 事 こそ さ ぶら へ 。 その 昔 、 あの 人 ど もの はぐくみ にて 有る べし と は 、 露 も 思ひ 寄候 はず 。 」 とて 、 御 涙 を 流さ せ 給 へ ば 、 附參 せ たる 女房 たち も 、 袖 を ぞぬら さ れ ける 。 女院 御 涙 を 押て 申させ 給ひ ける は 、 「 かかる 身 に なる 事 は 、 一旦 の 歎き 申す に 及び 候 はね ど も 、 後生 菩提 の 爲 に は 、 悦 と おぼえ さ ぶら ふ也 。 忽 に 釋迦 の 遺弟 に 列 なり 、 忝 なく 彌陀 の 本願 に 乘じ て 、 五 障 三 從 の 苦み を 遁れ 、 三 時 に 六根 を きよめ 、 一筋 に 九品 の 淨刹 を 願ふ 。 專 一門 の 菩提 を 祈り 、 常 は 三尊 の 來迎 を 期す 。 何 の 世 に も 忘がたき は 先帝 の 御 面影 、 忘れ ん と すれ ども わすら れ ず 、 し の ばん と すれ ども し の ば れ ず 。 唯恩 愛 の 道程 、 悲かり ける 事 は なし 。 されば 彼 菩提 の 爲 に 、 朝夕 の 勤め 怠る 事候 はず 。 是も 然 べき 善 知識 と こそ 覺 え候 へ 。 」 と 申させ 給ひ けれ ば 、 法皇 仰 せ なり ける は 、 「 此國 は 粟散 邊土 なり とい へ ども 、 忝く も 十善 の 餘薫 に 答 へ て 萬乘 の 主 と なり 、 隨分 一 と し て 心 に かな はず と いふ 事 なし 。 就中 佛法 流布 の 世 に 生 て 佛道 修行 の 志 あれ ば 、 後 生善 處 疑ある べ から ず 。 人間 の あだ なる 習 は 今更 驚く べき に は あら ねど 、 御有 樣 見奉る に 、 餘 に 爲方 なう こそ 候 へ 。 」 と 仰け れ ば 、 女院 重 て 申させ 給ひ ける は 、 「 我平 相國 の 娘 と し て 、 天子 の 國母 と なり しか ば 、 一天 四 海 皆 掌の まゝ なりき 。 拜禮 の 春 の 始 より 、 色々 の 衣 が へ 、 佛名 の 年 の 暮 、 攝禄 以下 の 大臣 公卿 に もて なさ れし 有樣 、 六 欲 四 禪 の 雲 の 上 にて 、 八 萬 の 諸天 に 圍繞 せ られ 候 ふらむ 樣 に 、 百官 悉く 仰ぬ 者 や 候ひ し 。 清凉 紫 宸 の 床 の 上 、 玉 の 簾 の 中 にて 持成 さ れ 、 春 は 南殿 の 櫻 に 心 を とめ て 日 を 暮し 、 九 夏 三 伏 の あつき 日 は 、 泉 を むすび て 心 を 慰み 、 秋 は 雲 の 上 の 月 を 獨見ん 事 許さ れ ず 、 玄冬 素雪 の 寒き 夜 は 、 つま を 重ね て 暖 にす 。 長生 不老 の 術 を 願ひ 、 蓬 莱 不死 の 藥 を 尋ね て も 、 唯久 し から ん 事 を のみ思 へり 。 明ても 、 暮れ て も 、 樂しみ 榮えし 事 、 天上 の 果報 も 、 是に は 過じ と こそ 覺え 候ひ し か 。 それ に 壽永 の 秋 の 初 、 木 曾義 仲 と か や に 恐れ て 、 一門 の 人々 住馴 し 都 を ば 雲井 の 餘所 に 顧み て 、 故郷 を 燒野 の 原 と 打詠め 、 古 は 名 のみ 聞し須磨 より 明石 の 浦傳ひ 、 さすが 哀れ に 覺え て 、 晝 は 漫々 たる 浪路 を 分て 袖 を ぬら し 、 夜 は 洲崎 の 千鳥 と 共 に 泣明 し 、 浦々 島々由 ある 所 を 見 しかど も 、 故郷 の 事 は わすら れ ず 。 かく て 寄る 方 無り し は 、 五衰 必滅 の 悲と こそ おぼえ 候し か 。 人間 の 事 は 、 愛別 離苦 、 怨憎 會 苦 、 共 に 、 吾身 に 知ら れ て 候ふ 。 四 苦 八 苦一 と し て 殘る 所候 はず 。 さても 筑前 國太 宰府 と 云處 にて 、 維義 と か や に 九 國 の 内 を も 追出さ れ 、 山野 廣 とい へ ども 立寄 休む べき 處 なし 。 同じ 秋 の 末 に も なり しか ば 、 昔 は 九 重 の 雲 の 上 にて 見し 月 を 、 今 は 八重 の 鹽路 に 詠め つ ゝ 、 明し暮 し 候ひ し 程 に 、 神無月 の 比ほひ 、 清經 の 中將 が 、 都 の うち を ば 源氏 が 爲 に 責落 さ れ 、 鎭西 を ば 維義 が 爲 に 追出 さる 。 網 に か ゝ れる 魚 の 如く 、 何く へ 行か ば遁る べき か は 。 存 へ 果べき 身 に も あら ず とて 、 海 に 沈み 候ひしぞ 心 憂き 事 の 始め にて 候ひ し 。 波 の 上 にて 日 を 暮し 、 船 の 中 にて 夜 を 明し 、 御 つぎ物 も なかり しか ば 、 供御 を 具ふる 人 も なし 。 適供 御 は 備 へん と すれ ども 水 なけれ ば 參ら ず 。 大海 に 浮ぶ とい へ ども 、 潮なれ ば 呑事 も なし 。 是又 餓 鬼 道 の 苦 と こそ お ぼえ 候ひ し か 。 かく て 室 山 水島 所々 の 戰ひ に 勝しか ば 、 人々 、 少色 なほて 見え 候ひ し 程 に 一谷 と いふ 處 にて 一門 多く 滅び し 後 は 直衣束 帶 を 引替 て 、 鐵 を の べ て 身 に 纒ひ 、 明て も 暮て も 、 軍よばひ の 聲斷ざり し 事 修羅 の 鬪 諍 、 帝釋 の 爭 ひも 、 かく や と こそ おぼえ 候ひ し か 。 一谷 を 攻落 さ れ て 後 、 親 は 子 に おく れ 、 妻 は 夫 に 別れ 、 沖 に 釣 する 船 を ば 、 敵 の 船 か と 肝 を 消し 、 遠き 松 に 、 群居 鷺 を ば 、 源氏 の 旗 か と 心 を 盡す 。 さても 門司 赤間 の 關 にて 軍 は 今日 を 限 と 見え しか ば 、 二 位 の 尼 申 おく 事 候ひき 。 『 男 の 生殘 らん 事 は 、 千萬 が 一 も 有難 し 。 縱又 遠き ゆかり は 自生 殘 たり と いふ と も 吾等 が 後世 を 弔 はん 事 も 有り が た し 。 昔 より 女 は 殺さ ぬ 習ひ なれ ば 如何 に もし て ながら へ て 主上 の 後世 を も 弔 ひまゐら せ 、 吾等 が 後世 を も 助け 給 へ 。 』 と 掻口 説き 申候ひ し が 、 夢 の 心地 し て おぼえ 候ひ し 程 に 風俄 に 吹き 、 浮雲厚く たなびい て 、 兵心 を 惑し 、 天運 盡 て 、 人 の 力 に 及び が たし 。 既に 今 は かう と 見え しか ば 、 二 位 の 尼 先 帝 を 抱き奉 て 船端 へ 出し 時 、 あき れ たる 御 樣 にて 『 尼ぜ 我 を ばいづち へ 具 し て 行ん と する ぞ 。 』 と 仰さ ぶらひし に 、 幼き 君 に 向ひ奉り 涙 を 押 へ て 申さぶらひし は 、 『 君 は 未だ 知し 召 さ れ候 はず や 。 先世 の 十善 戒行 の 御力 に 依 て 、 今萬 乘 の 主 と は 生れ さ せ 給 へ ども 、 惡縁 に 引か れ て 御運 既に 盡 給ひ ぬ 。 先づ 東 に 向 は せ 給 て 、 伊勢 大 神宮 に 御 暇 申させ 給ひ 、 其後 西方 淨土 の 來迎 に 預ら ん と 思食 し 、 西 に 向 は せ 給ひ て 御念 佛 候ふ べし 。 此國 は 粟散 邊土 と て 心 憂き 堺 にて さぶら へ ば 、 極樂 淨土 と て 、 め で たき 所 へ 具し 參 せ 候ふぞ 。 』 と 、 泣々 申 候ひ し かば 、 山鳩 色 の 御衣 に 鬟結 せ 給ひ て 、 御 涙 に 溺れ 、 小う 美くしい 御手 を 合せ 、 先づ 東 を 伏拜み 、 伊勢 大 神宮 に 御 暇 申させ 給ひ 、 其後 西 に 向は せ 給ひ て 御念 佛 あり しか ば 、 二 位 尼 やがて 抱き奉 て 海 に 沈み し 御 面影 目 も くれ 、 心 も 消果 て て 、 忘ん と すれ 共忘 られ ず 、 忍 ばん と すれ 共忍 ば れ ず 。 殘 留まる 人々 の を めき 叫び し 聲 、 叫喚 大叫 喚 の ほの ほ の 底 の 罪人 も 、 是れ に は 過じ と こそ 覺 候ひ し か 。 さて 武士 共 に とら は れ て 上り 候ひ し 時 に 、 播磨 國 明石 の 浦 に つい て 、 ちと 打目 睡 て 候ひ し 夢 に 、 昔 の 内裏 に は 遙 に 勝り たる 所 に 、 先帝 を 始奉 て 一門 の 公卿 殿 上 人 、 皆 ゆゆしげ なる 禮儀 にて 候ひ し を 、 都 を 出 て 後 、 かゝる 所 は 未だ 見ざり つる に 『 是はい づくぞ 。 』 と 問ひ 候ひ し か ば 、 二 位 の 尼 と 覺え て 『 龍 宮城 』 と 答 へ 候ひ し 時 『 目出 度かり ける 所 かな 。 是に は 苦 は 無き か 。 』 と 問候 ひしかば 、 『 龍畜 經 の 中 に 見え て 候ふ 、 能々 後世 を 弔ひ給 へ 。 』 と 申す と 覺え て 夢 覺 ぬ 。 其後 は い よ ／ ＼經 を 讀念 佛 し て 、 か の 御 菩提 を 弔奉る 。 是皆 六道 に た が はじ と こそ 覺 え候 へ 。 」 と 申させ 給 へ ば 、 法皇 仰 なり ける は 、 「 異國 の 玄弉 三 藏 は 、 悟り の 前 に 六道 を 見 、 吾朝 の 日藏 上人 は 、 藏王 權 現 の 御力 にて 、 六道 を 見 たり と こそ 承 は れ 。 是程 まの あたり に 御 覽 ぜ られ ける 御事 誠 に 有難う こそ 候 へ 。 」 とて 御 涙 に 咽ば せ給 へ ば 、 供奉 の 公卿 殿 上 人 も 皆 袖 を ぞ絞 られ ける 。 女院 も 御涙 を 流さ せ 給 へ ば 、 つき 參 せ たる 女房 達 も 又袖 を ぞぬら さ れ ける 。

Translation: "Weary of this world, I must surely suffer. Please grant me an immediate audience and return with haste." Upon hearing this, she was permitted to enter the Empress's hermitage. "Before the window of a single thought, I await the light of Amitabha's salvation; before the frail brushwood of ten recitations, I shall surely await the descent of the holy hosts. What a wonderful surprise this is!" Thus she said, and she was granted an audience. The Retired Emperor, seeing this scene, remarked, "In the eight hundred thousand kalpas of sorrow, I shall surely meet the sorrow of inevitable extinction. Even the six heavens of the Desire Realm have not yet escaped the sorrow of the Five Decays. The supreme bliss of the City of Good Vision, the lofty pavilion of the Intermediate Dhyana, and the bliss of transitory dreams and illusory retribution are all already in endless samsara, like a turning wheel. The sorrow of the Five Decays of the gods is also present for humans, is it not?" "Even so, who could ask such a question? Whatever the matter, one would surely think thus in ancient times," he replied. "No news has reached me from anywhere. Only Ryufu and Nobutaka's lady-in-waiting has sent word. In those days, I never even imagined that these people would be raised up." Thus saying, she shed tears, and the ladies-in-waiting who attended also wet their sleeves. The Empress, suppressing her tears, said, "Although it is not necessary to lament such a state of affairs for this life alone, for the sake of my future existence and enlightenment, I feel joy. I shall suddenly join the ranks of Shakyamuni's disciples, unworthily ride upon Amida's original vow, escape the sufferings of the Five Obstacles and Three Subserviences, purify the six sense organs in the three times, and single-mindedly aspire to the nine grades of the Pure Land. I pray for Bodhi with one-mindedness and always await the descent of the Three Jewels. What is most unforgettable in this world is the face of the Late Emperor; though I wish to forget him, I cannot; though I wish to suppress the memory, it cannot be suppressed. There is no sorrow in the path of affection and love. Therefore, for the sake of that Bodhi, I shall never be negligent in my morning and evening practices. I consider this to be a good teacher who is truly worthy." The Retired Emperor replied, "Although this land is but a remote land of millet seeds, I unworthily responded to the lingering fragrance of the Ten Virtues and became the sovereign of ten thousand chariots. In every respect, there is nothing that does not accord with my heart. Especially, having been born in an age where the Dharma spreads, and having the aspiration to cultivate the Buddha Way, there is no doubt of a good rebirth in the future. The nature of humans to be impermanent is no longer surprising, but seeing your state, it is truly extraordinary." The Empress replied again, "As the daughter of the Heike Chancellor and becoming the Mother of the Emperor, I held the entire world within my palm. From the beginning of spring when I paid my respects, through the changing of various robes, until the end of the year when I recited Buddha's names, the ministers and courtiers below the rank of Dainagon were all at my service. I was surrounded by eighty thousand heavenly beings as if on the clouds of the Four Dhyanas and the Six Desires. All officials bowed to me. On the bed of Seiryoden and Shishin, within the jade curtains, I was cared for. In spring, I stayed my heart on the cherry blossoms of the Southern Hall and spent the days. On the hot days of the three heats of summer, I tied springs to comfort my heart. In autumn, I was not permitted to gaze alone at the moon above the clouds. On the cold nights of the white snow of the black winter, I piled layers of clothes to keep warm. I wished for the art of life immortality and searched for the elixir of the Penglai immortals, thinking only of living long. Whether by day or by night, I felt that no joy or glory in the heavens could surpass this. Then, at the beginning of autumn in the year of Juei, fearing Kiso Yoshinaka and the like, I looked back at the capital where my clan had lived, no longer seeing it as anything but a clouded sky. I lamented my hometown as the plain of the Burning Fields. From the ancient place of Suma, where I had only heard the name, I traveled to Akashi Bay. Still, I felt great pity. By day, I divided my sleeve-wet path along the aimless waves; by night, I cried until dawn with the thousand birds of Sasaki. I visited many places, yet I could not forget my hometown. Thus, having nowhere to go, I felt the sorrow of inevitable extinction, the Five Decays. Human affairs include the suffering of separation from loved ones and the suffering of meeting those we hate. These are known to me personally. The Four Sufferings and Eight Sufferings are all present within me. Yet, at Dazaifu in Chikuzen Province, where I was driven out of the nine provinces by Minamoto no Yoritomo, though the mountains and fields were vast, there was no place to stop and rest. When the end of the same autumn came, I chanted while gazing at the moon I once saw from the nine-fold clouds of the palace, now in the eight-fold salt road, from morning to evening. Then, in the month without gods, Minamoto no Yoshitsune and the other general drove the Minamoto clan out of the capital and drove the Taira out of Chikuzen. Like fish caught in a net, where could I flee? I felt that I had no body to survive, and so I sank into the sea, the beginning of all sorrowful events. I spent days on the waves and nights in the boat. There was no provision, and no one to prepare offerings. I wished to prepare offerings, but there was no water to go and fetch. Even floating on the great sea, if the tide was high, I could not eat. I felt this was the suffering of the hungry ghost realm. Thus, after winning battles at Murasame, Shimoshima, and other places, when people looked slightly relieved, and after many of my clan perished at Ichi-no-Tani, I changed my court robes and armor, donning iron plates on my body. Whether by day or by night, the sound of military calls never ceased. I felt this was the struggle of the Asuras, the conflict of Indra. After Ichi-no-Tani was attacked and fallen, parents were left behind by children, wives separated from husbands. I mistook a boat fishing in the offing for an enemy ship, and my heart was consumed; I mistook a flock of herons on a distant pine for the Minamoto flag, and my heart was exhausted. Yet, when the army at Monji and Akama gate seemed to set today as their limit, the Lady of the Second Rank pleaded, 'It is extremely rare for a man to survive, even one in ten thousand. Even if distant relatives remain alive, it is precious for us to mourn our future. Since ancient times, women have not been killed. Please, by all means, save us so that we may also mourn the Late Emperor's future and help our own future.' She pleaded earnestly, and as if in a dream, the wind suddenly blew, thick floating clouds gathered, confused the soldiers' hearts, and the heavenly fortune ended, beyond human power. Since it was now clear that this was the case, the Lady of the Second Rank embraced the Late Emperor and carried him to the boat's edge. In a bewildered manner, he said, 'A nun! Where are you taking me?' Turning to the young prince, she suppressed her tears and replied, 'Has the Prince not yet understood? By the power of the Ten Virtues and precepts of your previous life, you were born as the sovereign of ten thousand chariots, but drawn by evil karmic connections, your fate has already ended. First, turn east, request leave from the Grand Shrine of Ise, and then, hoping to receive the descent of the Pure Land of the West, turn west and chant the Buddha's name. This land is but a remote border of millet seeds, a sorrowful place to stay. Therefore, we shall go to the blissful Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.' Thus she wept and spoke. The prince, with his hair styled in the color of mountain doves, drowned in tears, joined his small, beautiful hands, first bowed east, requested leave from the Grand Shrine of Ise, and then turned west and chanted the Buddha's name. The Lady of the Second Rank immediately embraced him and sank into the sea. His face, eyes, and heart were extinguished, yet I cannot forget him, nor can I endure the memory. The wailing and screaming of the remaining people, even the sinners at the bottom of the hot furnace of screaming and loud screaming, could not surpass this. Then, when captured by the warriors and brought ashore, arriving at Akashi Bay in Harima Province, I fell asleep for a moment and dreamed. In the dream, I saw a place far surpassing the former palace, where the Late Emperor, along with the courtiers and nobles of my clan, were all performing solemn rites. Having left the capital, I had never seen such a place before. When I asked, 'Where is this?' and the Lady of the Second Rank answered, 'The Dragon Palace,' I asked, 'What a joyous place! Is there no suffering here?' She replied, 'It appears in the Sutra of the Dragon Beasts. Please earnestly mourn our future.' Thus I awoke from the dream. Since then, I have diligently read sutras and chanted the Buddha's name to mourn that prince's soul. I consider this to be a path that will not deviate from the six realms.' Thus she spoke. The Retired Emperor replied, 'The Chinese monk Xuanzang saw the six realms before attaining enlightenment, and our own Dayzo Shonin saw the six realms through the power of the King of the Treasure. To witness such things firsthand is truly wonderful.' Thus he choked with tears, and the courtiers and nobles who attended also wrung out their sleeves. The Empress also shed tears, and the ladies-in-waiting who attended also wet their sleeves.

Comment: The phrase '粟散邊土' (sussan hentō) alludes to the Buddhist cosmological concept of 'sūcī-dvīpa' (a land of scattered seeds or atoms), used here to contrast the imperial authority ('万乗の主') with the humble, transient nature of the earthly realm. This specific terminology underscores the theological pivot in the Empress's speech: despite her former status as the daughter of the Heike and mother of the Emperor, she now views the 'Heian' capital not as a center of power but as a mere stepping stone toward the Pure Land, reinforcing the 'impermanence' (mujō) theme central to the Heike Monogatari's narrative arc. The passage '一谷を攻落されて後、親は子におくれ、妻は夫に別れ' employs a specific rhetorical structure known as 'gōkō' (parallelism) where the syntactic inversion ('parent behind child', 'wife separates from husband') serves to heighten the emotional impact of the disaster at Ichi-no-Tani. This is not merely a description of death but a deliberate literary device to invert natural social hierarchies and familial bonds, reflecting the chaos of the Heian period's collapse and the Buddhist concept of 'mappō' (the age of the decline of the Dharma).

さる 程 に 寂光 院 の 鐘の 聲 、 今日 も 暮ぬ と 打し られ 、 夕陽 西 に 傾け ば 、 御名 殘 惜う は おぼし けれども 、 御 涙 を 押 て 還御 なら せ給ひけり 。 女院 は 今更 古 を 思食 し 出さ せ 給ひ て 、 忍あ へ ぬ 御 涙 に 、 袖 の 柵 塞あ へ さ せ給 はず 。 遙 に 御 覽じ 送ら せ給ひ て 、 還御 も やう ／ ＼延 さ せ 給ひけれ ば 、 御 本尊 に 向ひ 奉り 、 「 先帝 聖 靈 、 一門 亡 魂 、 成等 正覺 、 頓證 菩提 。 」 と 泣々 祈ら せ給ひけり 。 昔 は 東 に 向 は せ 給ひ て 「 伊勢 大 神宮 、 正 八幡 大 菩薩 、 天子 寶算 、 千秋 萬 歳 。 」 と 申させ 給ひ し に 、 今 は 引か へ て 、 西 に 向ひ 手 を 合せ 「 過去 聖 靈 、 一 佛 淨土 へ 。 」 と 祈ら せ給ふ こそ 悲しけれ 。 御 寢 所 の 障子 に かう ぞ遊 さ れ ける 。

Translation: So it was that the bell of Jikkō-in temple struck, announcing today's end as well; when the evening sun slanted westward, though she wished to linger in farewell, she restrained her tears and departed. The retired empress now began to recall the past, and with tears she could not bear, she could not keep her sleeves dry. She gazed afar and sent them off, and since her return was delayed in various ways, she turned toward her principal image and prayed, with weeping: 'May the holy spirit of the former Emperor, and the souls of the clan, attain perfect enlightenment, and suddenly realize Bodhi.' In days past she had turned east and said, 'Ise Grand Shrine, Hachiman Daibosatsu, may the Emperor's reign last a thousand autumns and ten thousand years,' but now she turned and faced west, clasping her hands and praying, 'To the holy spirits of the past, to the Pure Land of One Buddha.' This is indeed sorrowful. She had gone to her sleeping quarters and there had her screens drawn.

So it was that the bell of Jikkō-in temple struck, announcing today's end as well; when the evening sun slanted westward, though she wished to linger in farewell, she restrained her tears and departed. The retired empress now began to recall the past, and with tears she could not bear, she could not keep her sleeves dry. She gazed afar and sent them off, and since her return was delayed in various ways, she turned toward her principal image and prayed, with weeping: 'May the holy spirit of the former Emperor, and the souls of the clan, attain perfect enlightenment, and suddenly realize Bodhi.' In days past she had turned east and said, 'Ise Grand Shrine, Hachiman Daibosatsu, may the Emperor's reign last a thousand autumns and ten thousand years,' but now she turned and faced west, clasping her hands and praying, 'To the holy spirits of the past, to the Pure Land of One Buddha.' This is indeed sorrowful. She had gone to her sleeping quarters and there had her screens drawn.

Comment: The term '寂光院' (Jakō-in) functions here as a specific metonym for the Pure Land (Sukhāvatī) in the context of the Taira clan's defeat, yet it simultaneously refers to the actual temple in Uji where the retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa resided. The commentary must distinguish between the geographical reality of the temple (where the Empress Dowager is physically located) and the theological allusion to the 'Land of Bliss' that the text evokes through the sound of the bell and the direction of the prayer, a duality central to the Heike's narrative strategy of merging historical tragedy with Buddhist soteriology.

See notes

  • Comment: The term '寂光院' (Jakō-in) functions here as a specific metonym for the Pure Land (Sukhāvatī) in the context of the Taira clan's defeat, yet it simultaneously refers to the actual temple in Uji where the retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa resided. The commentary must distinguish between the geographical reality of the temple (where the Empress Dowager is physically located) and the theological allusion to the 'Land of Bliss' that the text evokes through the sound of the bell and the direction of the prayer, a duality central to the Heike's narrative strategy of merging historical tragedy with Buddhist soteriology. — Comment_type: Literary and Rhetorical Commentary

御幸 の 御供 に 候 は れける 徳大 寺 左 大臣 實定 公 、 御 庵 室 の 柱 に 書附 られ ける と か や 。

Translation: The Minister of the Left, Sadasuke of the Tokudaiji family, who had been in attendance on the imperial progress, was said to have been written upon the pillar of her hermitage, is it not?

See notes

The Minister of the Left, Sadasuke of the Tokudaiji family, who had been in attendance on the imperial progress, was said to have been written upon the pillar of her hermitage, is it not?

Comment: The sentence employs the archaic passive construction '書附られ' (sho-tsukura-re), derived from the compound verb '書附く' (sho-tsuku, to write on/inscribe upon) in the passive voice, followed by the perfective auxiliary 'ける' (keru). While '書附く' is attested in Heian literature, its passive form here is syntactically marked, emphasizing the involuntary or fated nature of the inscription appearing on the pillar, a nuance crucial for interpreting the supernatural or karmic tone of the episode where the text is discovered rather than written by the subject's hand.

こし 方行 末 の 事共 覺しめ し續け て 、 御 涙 に 咽ば せ給 ふ折 し も 、 山郭 公音 信け れ ば 、 女 院

Translation: Having been made aware of the matter of the course of events, and continuing to make him choke with tears, just as that was happening, the Mountain Nightingale's voice was heard, and the Lady-in-Waiting

See notes

Having been made aware of the matter of the course of events, and continuing to make him choke with tears, just as that was happening, the Mountain Nightingale's voice was heard, and the Lady-in-Waiting

Comment: The sentence hinges on the term 山郭公 (yama-kakko), a personification of the mountain cuckoo (hototogisu). In the Heike Monogatari, the bird's cry is not merely a naturalistic detail but a specific narrative trigger: its call signifies the passage of time and the impermanence of the human world, often precipitating a shift in the emotional register of the scene. Here, the weeping of the female院 (likely the retired Empress Genshō or a similar high-ranking figure) is interrupted by the bird, a classic *mono no aware* device where nature intrudes upon human sentiment to underscore the transience of the moment. The syntax '音信ければ' (having heard the sound) functions as a causal participle, linking the external auditory stimulus directly to the internal emotional state of the courtiers, a structural feature characteristic of the Heike's oral-performance aesthetic.

See notes

抑壇 の 浦 にて 生 ながら 捕ら れ し 人々 は 大路 を 渡し て 頭 を はね られ 、 妻子 に 離れ て 遠流 せ らる 。 池大 納言 の 外 は 一人 も 命 を 生け られ ず 、 都 に 置か れ ず 。 されど も 四 十 餘 人 の 女房 達 の 御事 は 、 沙汰 に も [ 1 ] 及ば さり しか ば 、 親類 に 從ひ 縁 に 就い て ぞお は し ける 。 上 は 玉の 簾 の 中 まで も 、 風 靜 なる 家 も なく 、 下 は 柴の とぼ その もと まで も 塵 收 れる 宿 も なし 。 枕 を 雙 べし 妹 背 も 、 雲井 の 餘所 に ぞ成 果る 。 養ひ立し 親子 も 、 行方 知ら ず 別れ けり 。 忍ぶ 思ひ は 盡せ ね ども 、 嘆 ながら も さて こそ 過 さ れ けれ 。 是 は 只 入道 相國 、 一 天 四 海 を 掌 に 握 て 上 は 一人 を も 恐れ ず 、 下 は 萬民 を も 顧み ず 、 死罪 流刑 、 思ふ 樣 に 行ひ 、 世 を も人 を も憚か られ ざり し が 致す 所 なり 。 父祖 の 罪業 は 子孫 に 報ふ と 云ふ 事疑 な し とぞ 見え たり ける 。

Translation: Indeed, the people who were captured alive at Dan-no-ura were led across the main road, their heads severed, separated from their wives and children, and exiled to distant lands. Except for the Dainagon Ike, not a single life was spared, nor was anyone left in the capital. However, as the affairs of the forty or more court ladies did not even warrant consideration, they followed their relatives and, according to their circumstances, went into exile. Above, even within the jade curtains, there was no home without wind; below, even at the base of the brushwood piles, there was no lodging without dust. Even the sisters who shared a pillow, the 'Mise', were scattered to distant places. Parents and children who had been raised together were parted, their whereabouts unknown. Though the longing heart could not be exhausted, sighing and yet enduring, it was indeed so. This was the result of the Great Minister, the one who, holding the four seas in his palm, feared no one above and cared for no commoner below, who committed capital punishment and exile at his will, sparing neither the world nor people. It appears that there is no doubt that the sins of fathers and ancestors are repaid to their descendants.

See notes

Comment: The phrase '沙汰にも及ばさり' employs the archaic negative auxiliary 'さる' (sar) attached to the compound '及ばす' (obasus, negative potential of '及ぶ'), which here functions as a passive/periphrastic form meaning 'to be dealt with' or 'to be subjected to official scrutiny.' The construction '沙汰に及ぶ' is a specific bureaucratic idiom denoting that a case has reached the stage of formal adjudication by the authorities. The use of the negative '及ばさり' (obasari) in this context signifies that the female attendants were explicitly excluded from the standard judicial process of the Taira purge, sparing them from the '沙汰' (official sentencing) that befell the men. This grammatical structure highlights the distinction between the 'official' fate of the male warriors and the 'unofficial' or administrative fate of the women, who were dispersed rather than formally tried.

See notes

かく て 年月 を 過させ 給ふ 程 に 、 女院 御 心地 例 なら ず 渡ら せ 給ひしかば 、 中尊 の 御手 の 五 色 の 絲 を 引 へ つゝ 、 「 南 無 西方 極 樂 世界 教主 彌 陀如 來 必ず 引攝 し 給 へ 。 」 とて 御念 佛 有し かば 、 大納 言佐 局 阿波 内侍 左右 に 候 て 、 今 を 限り の 悲しさ に 聲 を 惜 まず 泣き 叫ぶ 。 御念 佛 の 聲 やう やう よ わら せ まし まし けれ ば 西 に 紫雲 靉 靆き 、 異香 室 に みち 、 音 樂空 に 聞ゆ 。 限 ある 事 なれ ば 、 建久 二 年 き さらぎ の 中旬 に 一 期 遂 に 終ら せ 給ひ ぬ 。 きさい の 宮 の 御 位 より 片時 も 離れ まゐ らせ ず し て 候 は れ給 し かば 、 御 臨終 の 御 時 、 別路 に 迷ひ し も 遣方 なく ぞおぼえ ける 。 此 女房 達 は 、 昔 の 草 の ゆかり も 枯果 て 、 よる 方 も なき 身 なれ ども 、 折々 の 御 佛 事 營 み給 ふぞ哀 なる 。 終 に 彼 人々 は 、 龍女 が 正覺 の 跡 を おひ 、 韋 提希 夫人 の 如 に 、 皆 往生 の 素懷 を 遂ける とぞ 聞え し 。

Translation: Thus, as time passed and the lady-in-waiting's health deteriorated beyond the norm, she took to drawing upon the five-colored silk threads of the Great Consecrated One, chanting, 'Namu Amida Nyorai, be sure to draw me into your embrace.' As she prayed with a voice growing increasingly weak, the Great Minister Sa's chambermaid and Awano no Naishi stood on either side of her, weeping and crying out without sparing their voices in their grief at this final sorrow. As her prayer grew faint, purple clouds gathered in the west, filling the room with a strange fragrance, and music was heard in the sky. Since all things are limited, in the middle of the second month of the second year of Kenkyū, her life finally came to an end. She never left the side of the Prince Kisa's palace for even a moment, and at the time of her death, she was said to have become lost on a separate path, with no one to guide her. These ladies-in-waiting, though their ties to the past had withered and they were now without even a home to call their own, found it deeply sorrowful to see her constantly perform Buddhist rites. Ultimately, it is said that those people followed in the footsteps of the Dragon Girl attaining perfect enlightenment, and like Lady Vaitāli, all accomplished their original aspiration for rebirth.

See notes

Comment: The phrase '中尊の御手の五色の絲を引へつゝ' (holding the five-colored thread of the Hand of Chūson) refers specifically to the 'Hōshō' (Blessing) ritual associated with the deathbed of Empress Shigeko (later Empress Kenreimon'in), who was the daughter of Taira no Kiyomori. While 'Chūson' generally refers to the temple Chūson-ji in Hiraizumi (famous for the Konjikidō), in this specific context of the Kenreimon'in's death, it alludes to the 'Hōshō' thread tradition where a colored thread is held by the dying person, symbolizing the connection to Amida Buddha and the Pure Land. The specific invocation of the 'five-colored thread' here is a ritualistic detail marking the transition from the 'Hōshō' ceremony to the final moments, distinguishing it from generic deathbed descriptions in other Heike texts. The phrase '建久二年きさらぎの中旬' (mid-February of the second year of Kenkyū) provides a precise chronological anchor. Empress Kenreimon'in (Shigeko) died on February 15, 1191 (Kenkyū 2, 2nd month, 15th day). The text's 'mid-February' is not merely an approximation but a specific reference to the historical date of her death, which is crucial for the historiographical function of the *Heike Monogatari*. The use of 'きさらぎ' (kisaragi) instead of the more common '二月' (nigatsu) is a stylistic choice typical of the *Heike* to evoke a classical, poetic tone, but the specific alignment with the historical death date of the Kenreimon'in (a major historical figure) serves to validate the narrative's claim to historical truth, a key rhetorical strategy in the epic.

See notes
